references.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
references.title: Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease.
references.finding: Vitamin D3 2000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years did not lower invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events (VITAL).

references.authors: Neale RE, Baxter C, Romero BD et al.
references.title: The D-Health Trial: a randomised controlled trial of the effect of vitamin D on mortality.
references.finding: D-Health: 60,000 IU vitamin D3 monthly for 5 years did not reduce all-cause mortality (HR 1.04, 0.93-1.18); cancer mortality was numerically higher.

references.authors: Thompson B, Waterhouse M, English DR et al.
references.title: Vitamin D supplementation and major cardiovascular events: D-Health randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: D-Health: monthly vitamin D3 gave a borderline 9% lower rate of major cardiovascular events (HR 0.91, 0.81-1.01; NNT 172 over 5 years).

references.authors: Bischoff-Ferrari HA, Vellas B, Rizzoli R et al.
references.title: Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation, Omega-3 Fatty Acid Supplementation, or a Strength-Training Exercise Program on Clinical Outcomes in Older Adults: The DO-HEALTH Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: DO-HEALTH: vitamin D3 2000 IU/day, omega-3 1 g/day or home exercise for 3 years had no significant benefit on blood pressure, physical performance, cognition, fractures or infections.

references.authors: Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration/EPIC-CVD/Vitamin D Studies Collaboration
references.title: Estimating dose-response relationships for vitamin D with coronary heart disease, stroke, and all-cause mortality: observational and Mendelian randomisation analyses.
references.finding: RETRACTED (2023 expression of concern, 2024 retraction and republication): original non-linear MR analysis that suggested vitamin D deficiency causally raised mortality; the residual stratification method was found to be biased.

references.authors: Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration/EPIC-CVD/Vitamin D Studies Collaboration
references.title: Estimating dose-response relationships for vitamin D with coronary heart disease, stroke, and all-cause mortality: observational and Mendelian randomisation analyses.
references.finding: Republished analysis using corrected non-linear MR methods: genetically predicted 25(OH)D had no association with coronary disease, stroke or all-cause mortality at any 25(OH)D level, including deficiency.

references.authors: Sutherland JP, Zhou A, Hyppönen E
references.title: Vitamin D Deficiency Increases Mortality Risk in the UK Biobank : A Nonlinear Mendelian Randomization Study.
references.finding: Non-linear MR using the residual method reported an L-shaped causal effect of low 25(OH)D on mortality (OR 1.25 at 25 vs 50 nmol/L); it relies on the stratification method later shown to be biased for vitamin D.

references.authors: Burgess S
references.title: Violation of the Constant Genetic Effect Assumption Can Result in Biased Estimates for Non-Linear Mendelian Randomization.
references.finding: Showed the residual method for non-linear MR assumes a constant genetic effect that is violated for 25(OH)D (five-fold variation across deciles); the protective effect of vitamin D in deficient people appeared with the residual method but not the doubly ranked method.

references.authors: Wang Y, Sha S, Gwenzi T et al.
references.title: Impact of vitamin D supplementation on all-cause mortality: Randomized trials revisited.
references.finding: Target-trial emulation of VITAL and D-Health in UK Biobank reproduced the null trial results in replete populations but predicted HR 0.75-0.85 for mortality if the same 25(OH)D rise were given to insufficient or deficient people (observational, modelled).

references.authors: Wang Y, Sha S, Gwenzi T et al.
references.title: Effect of vitamin D supplementation on cardiovascular outcomes: randomized trials revisited.
references.finding: Same emulation for cardiovascular outcomes: predicted cardiovascular mortality HR 0.74-0.79 in people with low 25(OH)D; relies on observational 25(OH)D-outcome associations.

references.authors: Autier P, Boniol M, Pizot C et al.
references.title: Vitamin D status and ill health: a systematic review.
references.finding: Strong inverse associations of 25(OH)D with many diseases in cohorts were not reproduced by trials, even in people starting below 50 nmol/L; concluded low 25(OH)D is mainly a marker of ill health (reverse causation, inflammation).

references.authors: Demay MB, Pittas AG, Bikle DD et al.
references.title: Vitamin D for the Prevention of Disease: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline.
references.finding: Endocrine Society 2024: suggests against empiric vitamin D above the DRI for healthy adults under 75 and against routine 25(OH)D testing; suggests empiric supplementation for children, adults over 75, pregnancy and high-risk prediabetes.

references.authors: Hu KL, Liao T, Wu Q et al.
references.title: Vitamin D supplementation before in vitro fertilisation in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: multicentre, double blind, placebo controlled, randomised clinical trial.
references.finding: Multicentre double-blind RCT: vitamin D 4000 IU/day for up to 90 days before IVF raised 25(OH)D from ~16 to 32 ng/mL but did not raise live birth after first transfer (52.0% vs 50.2%; RR 1.03, 0.91-1.18).

references.authors: Somigliana E, Sarais V, Reschini M et al.
references.title: Single oral dose of vitamin D(3) supplementation prior to in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer in normal weight women: the SUNDRO randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: SUNDRO: a single 600,000 IU vitamin D3 dose before IVF did not improve clinical pregnancy (37% vs 40%; RR 0.91, 0.75-1.11) in any subgroup, including low baseline 25(OH)D.

references.authors: Iliuta F, Pijoan JI, Matorras R
references.title: Is the association of replete status in vitamin D with better results in IVF demonstrated?
references.finding: Letter to Human Reproduction questioning whether the association of replete vitamin D status with better IVF results had been demonstrated.

references.authors: Chu J, Gallos I, Tobias A, et al.
references.title: Vitamin D and assisted reproductive treatment outcome: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Vitamin D-replete women undergoing ART had higher live birth than deficient/insufficient women (OR 1.33); no association with miscarriage.

references.authors: Zhou X, Wu X, Luo X, et al.
references.title: Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation on In Vitro Fertilization Outcomes: A Trial Sequential Meta-Analysis of 5 Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: In vitamin D-deficient infertile women, supplementation raised chemical pregnancy (RR 1.53) but not clinical pregnancy (RR 1.34, NS) or embryo quality.

references.authors: Blomberg Jensen M, Lawaetz JG, Petersen JH, et al.
references.title: Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation on Semen Quality, Reproductive Hormones, and Live Birth Rate: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: Vitamin D (300,000 IU then 1400 IU/day) plus calcium for 150 days did not improve semen quality in vitamin-D-insufficient infertile men.

references.authors: Berry D, Wathen JK, Newell M
references.title: Bayesian model averaging in meta-analysis: vitamin E supplementation and mortality.
references.finding: Bayesian model-averaging re-analysis of the vitamin E dose-mortality trials concluded vitamin E intake is unlikely to affect mortality regardless of dose.

references.authors: Abner EL, Schmitt FA, Mendiondo MS et al.
references.title: Vitamin E and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis.
references.finding: Vitamin E supplementation for at least one year had no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 1.00, 0.98-1.02) and no dose-response up to 5,500 IU/day.

references.authors: Blumberg JB, Frei B
references.title: Why clinical trials of vitamin E and cardiovascular diseases may be fatally flawed. Commentary on "The relationship between dose of vitamin E and suppression of oxidative stress in humans".
references.finding: Commentary arguing that vitamin E cardiovascular trials may be fatally flawed because they did not confirm that the doses used actually lowered oxidative stress.

references.authors: Bjelakovic G, Nikolova D, Gluud LL, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various diseases.
references.finding: Antioxidant supplements increased mortality in low-bias trials (RR 1.04); beta-carotene (RR 1.05) and vitamin E (RR 1.03) significantly, vitamin C and selenium not.

references.authors: Miller ER 3rd, Pastor-Barriuso R, Dalal D, et al.
references.title: Meta-analysis: high-dosage vitamin E supplementation may increase all-cause mortality.
references.finding: High-dose vitamin E (>=400 IU/d) increased all-cause mortality by 39 per 10,000; risk rose above ~150 IU/d.

references.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force, Mangione CM, Barry MJ, et al.
references.title: Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
references.finding: USPSTF recommends against beta-carotene or vitamin E for preventing CVD or cancer (grade D); evidence is insufficient for multivitamins and other single or paired nutrients.

references.authors: Klein EA, Thompson IM Jr, Tangen CM, et al.
references.title: Vitamin E and the risk of prostate cancer: the Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT).
references.finding: With extended follow-up, vitamin E 400 IU/d significantly increased prostate cancer risk (HR 1.17).

references.authors: Virtamo J, Taylor PR, Kontto J et al.
references.title: Effects of α-tocopherol and β-carotene supplementation on cancer incidence and mortality: 18-year postintervention follow-up of the Alpha-tocopherol, Beta-carotene Cancer Prevention Study.
references.finding: ATBC post-trial follow-up: the excess lung cancer from beta-carotene disappeared after supplementation stopped (RR 1.04, 0.96-1.11); post-trial mortality was not significantly raised (RR 1.02).

references.authors: Goodman GE, Thornquist MD, Balmes J et al.
references.title: The Beta-Carotene and Retinol Efficacy Trial: incidence of lung cancer and cardiovascular disease mortality during 6-year follow-up after stopping beta-carotene and retinol supplements.
references.finding: CARET 6-year post-intervention follow-up: excess lung cancer (RR 1.12) and all-cause mortality (RR 1.08) persisted though no longer significant, with larger excess in women.

references.authors: Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group
references.title: The effect of vitamin E and beta carotene on the incidence of lung cancer and other cancers in male smokers.
references.finding: Beta-carotene 20 mg/d increased lung cancer incidence by 18% and total mortality by 8%; alpha-tocopherol 50 mg/d did not reduce lung cancer and was linked to more hemorrhagic-stroke deaths.

references.authors: Omenn GS, Goodman GE, Thornquist MD, et al.
references.title: Effects of a combination of beta carotene and vitamin A on lung cancer and cardiovascular disease.
references.finding: Beta-carotene 30 mg + retinol 25,000 IU increased lung cancer (RR 1.28) and all-cause mortality (RR 1.17); stopped early.

references.authors: Luo J, le Cessie S, van Heemst D et al.
references.title: Diet-Derived Circulating Antioxidants and Risk of Coronary Heart Disease: A Mendelian Randomization Study.
references.finding: Mendelian randomization: genetically higher circulating retinol, beta-carotene, lycopene, vitamin C (ascorbate) or tocopherols were not associated with coronary heart disease.

references.authors: Ferraro PM, Curhan GC, Gambaro G et al.
references.title: Total, Dietary, and Supplemental Vitamin C Intake and Risk of Incident Kidney Stones.
references.n: 3 US cohorts (HPFS, NHS I, NHS II)
references.finding: Supplemental vitamin C of 1000 mg/day or more was associated with modestly higher kidney-stone risk in men (HR 1.19) but not women; total intake 1000 mg/day+ HR 1.43 in men.

references.authors: Thomas LD, Elinder CG, Tiselius HG, et al.
references.title: Ascorbic acid supplements and kidney stone incidence among men: a prospective study.
references.finding: Use of ascorbic acid supplements (~1,000 mg tablets) was associated with about double the risk of kidney stones (RR 1.95).

references.authors: Lamontagne F, Masse MH, Menard J et al.
references.title: Intravenous Vitamin C in Adults with Sepsis in the Intensive Care Unit.
references.finding: LOVIT: intravenous vitamin C (50 mg/kg every 6 h) raised death or persistent organ dysfunction at 28 days (44.5% vs 38.5%; RR 1.21).

references.authors: Yeung LK, Alschuler DM, Wall M et al.
references.title: Multivitamin Supplementation Improves Memory in Older Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: Online COSMOS substudy: a daily multivitamin improved immediate word-list recall at 1 year (primary) and over 3 years, with no effect on secondary cognitive outcomes.

references.authors: Baker LD, Manson JE, Rapp SR et al.
references.title: Effects of cocoa extract and a multivitamin on cognitive function: A randomized clinical trial.
references.finding: Daily multivitamin improved global cognition by 0.07 SD over 3 years versus placebo; cocoa extract had no effect.

references.authors: Vyas CM, Manson JE, Sesso HD, et al.
references.title: Effect of multivitamin-mineral supplementation versus placebo on cognitive function: results from the clinic subcohort of the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial and meta-analysis of 3 cognitive studies within COSMOS.
references.n: 573 COSMOS-Clinic participants plus meta-analysis of 3 COSMOS cohorts
references.finding: A multivitamin improved episodic memory over 2 years; pooled COSMOS data showed small benefits on global cognition (0.07 SD).

references.authors: Loftfield E, O'Connell CP, Abnet CC, et al.
references.title: Multivitamin Use and Mortality Risk in 3 Prospective US Cohorts.
references.finding: Daily multivitamin use was not associated with lower mortality (HR 1.04 in the first half of follow-up).

references.authors: Chavarro JE, Rich-Edwards JW, Rosner BA, et al.
references.title: Use of multivitamins, intake of B vitamins, and risk of ovulatory infertility.
references.finding: Multivitamin use 6+ times a week was associated with 41% lower ovulatory infertility (RR 0.59), partly explained by folic acid.

references.authors: Sesso HD, Rist PM, Aragaki AK, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer and cardiovascular disease: the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial.
references.finding: A daily multivitamin for a median 3.6 years did not reduce total cancer (HR 0.97) or CVD (HR 0.98); lung cancer was lower (HR 0.62).

references.authors: Gaziano JM, Sesso HD, Christen WG, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: A daily multivitamin for 11 years modestly reduced total cancer (HR 0.92).

references.authors: Larsson SC, Traylor M, Malik R et al.
references.title: Modifiable pathways in Alzheimer's disease: Mendelian randomisation analysis.
references.finding: Mendelian randomization of 24 modifiable factors: genetically predicted homocysteine, serum folate and vitamin B12 were not associated with Alzheimer disease; education was.

references.authors: Clarke R, Bennett D, Parish S, et al.
references.title: Effects of homocysteine lowering with B vitamins on cognitive aging: meta-analysis of 11 trials with cognitive data on 22,000 individuals.
references.finding: Lowering homocysteine by about 25% with B vitamins had no effect on global or domain-specific cognitive aging, excluding benefits larger than 1 month per year.

references.authors: Smith AD, Smith SM, de Jager CA, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine-lowering by B vitamins slows the rate of accelerated brain atrophy in mild cognitive impairment: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: VITACOG: folic acid 0.8 mg, B6 20 mg and B12 0.5 mg daily for 2 years slowed brain atrophy (0.76% vs 1.08%/year) and by 53% in those with homocysteine above 13 umol/L.

references.authors: Garrard P, Jacoby R
references.title: B-vitamin trials meta-analysis: less than meets the eye.
references.finding: Letter titled "B-vitamin trials meta-analysis: less than meets the eye", disputing the conclusions of the Clarke 11-trial meta-analysis.

references.authors: Smith AD, Refsum H, Bottiglieri T, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine and Dementia: An International Consensus Statement.
references.finding: International consensus (Bradford Hill criteria): elevated plasma homocysteine is a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline, dementia and Alzheimer disease in older people.

references.authors: Dostal AM, Samavat H, Bedell S et al.
references.title: The safety of green tea extract supplementation in postmenopausal women at risk for breast cancer: results of the Minnesota Green Tea Trial.
references.finding: Minnesota Green Tea Trial: green tea extract with 843 mg EGCG/day for 1 year raised ALT in 6.7% vs 0.7% on placebo, with 1.3% having ALT-related serious adverse events.

references.authors: Acosta L, Byham-Gray L, Kurzer M et al.
references.title: Hepatotoxicity with High-Dose Green Tea Extract: Effect of Catechol-O-Methyltransferase and Uridine 5'-Diphospho-glucuronosyltransferase 1A4 Genotypes.
references.finding: In the Minnesota Green Tea Trial, the UGT1A4 rs6755571 A/C genotype was linked to much larger ALT rises (+78-82% vs +28-30%) on 843 mg/day EGCG.

references.authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS), Younes M, Aggett P, et al.
references.title: Scientific opinion on the safety of green tea catechins.
references.finding: Brewed green tea is generally safe (90-300 mg EGCG/day typical); supplement intakes >= 800 mg EGCG/day significantly raise serum transaminases in trials.

references.authors: Wiel C, Le Gal K, Ibrahim MX et al.
references.title: BACH1 Stabilization by Antioxidants Stimulates Lung Cancer Metastasis.
references.finding: In mice, long-term NAC and vitamin E promoted KRAS-driven lung cancer metastasis by stabilising BACH1 and switching on glycolysis.

references.authors: Bairati I, Meyer F, Gélinas M, et al.
references.title: A randomized trial of antioxidant vitamins to prevent second primary cancers in head and neck cancer patients.
references.finding: Alpha-tocopherol (with beta-carotene initially) during and after radiotherapy raised second primary cancers during supplementation (HR 2.88).

references.authors: Ambrosone CB, Zirpoli GR, Hutson AD, et al.
references.title: Dietary Supplement Use During Chemotherapy and Survival Outcomes of Patients With Breast Cancer Enrolled in a Cooperative Group Clinical Trial (SWOG S0221).
references.n: 1134 women with breast cancer in a chemotherapy trial
references.finding: Antioxidant supplement use before and during chemotherapy was associated with higher recurrence (adjHR 1.41, CI 0.98-2.04); B12 and iron use were significantly linked to worse outcomes.

references.authors: Sayin VI, Ibrahim MX, Larsson E, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants accelerate lung cancer progression in mice.
references.finding: NAC and vitamin E accelerated lung tumour progression and shortened survival in mice by reducing ROS, DNA damage and p53 expression.

references.authors: Pilling LC, Tamosauskaite J, Jones G et al.
references.title: Common conditions associated with hereditary haemochromatosis genetic variants: cohort study in UK Biobank.
references.finding: HFE C282Y homozygosity, a genetic cause of lifelong iron loading, was associated with more liver disease, arthritis and diabetes (OR 1.53 in men) and more incident morbidity.

references.authors: Daghlas I, Gill D
references.title: Genetically predicted iron status and life expectancy.
references.n: Mendelian randomization using parental lifespan GWAS
references.finding: Each SD of genetically higher serum iron corresponded to 0.7 fewer years of parental lifespan and lower odds of reaching the 90th age percentile (OR 0.81).

references.authors: Hansen R, Sejer EPF, Holm C, et al.
references.title: Iron supplements in pregnant women with normal iron status: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Daily iron in iron-replete pregnant women probably reduced iron-deficiency anaemia at term and low birthweight.

references.authors: Gencer B, Djousse L, Al-Ramady OT et al.
references.title: Effect of Long-Term Marine ɷ-3 Fatty Acids Supplementation on the Risk of Atrial Fibrillation in Randomized Controlled Trials of Cardiovascular Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Marine omega-3 supplements increased atrial fibrillation (HR 1.25, 1.07-1.46), more at >1 g/day (HR 1.49); each extra 1 g/day raised AF risk by 11%.

references.authors: Bhatt DL, Steg PG, Miller M et al.
references.title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia.
references.finding: REDUCE-IT: icosapent ethyl 4 g/day cut major cardiovascular events (HR 0.75) versus a mineral-oil placebo, with more AF hospitalisation (3.1% vs 2.1%) and borderline more serious bleeding (2.7% vs 2.1%).

references.authors: Ridker PM, Rifai N, MacFadyen J et al.
references.title: Effects of Randomized Treatment With Icosapent Ethyl and a Mineral Oil Comparator on Interleukin-1β, Interleukin-6, C-Reactive Protein, Oxidized Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol, Homocysteine, Lipoprotein(a), and Lipoprotein-Associated Phospholipase A2: A REDUCE-IT Biomarker Substudy.
references.finding: In REDUCE-IT, inflammatory and atherogenic biomarkers (hs-CRP +21.9%, IL-1beta +28.9%, LDL +10.9%) rose in the mineral-oil placebo arm, so part of the between-group difference reflects placebo-arm worsening.

references.authors: Nicholls SJ, Lincoff AM, Garcia M et al.
references.title: Effect of High-Dose Omega-3 Fatty Acids vs Corn Oil on Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Patients at High Cardiovascular Risk: The STRENGTH Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: STRENGTH: 4 g/day omega-3 carboxylic acids (EPA+DHA) versus corn oil did not reduce major cardiovascular events (HR 0.99); stopped for futility.

references.authors: Javaid M, Kadhim K, Bawamia B, et al.
references.title: Bleeding Risk in Patients Receiving Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
references.finding: Omega-3 PUFAs did not increase bleeding overall (RR 1.09, 0.91-1.31); high-dose purified EPA raised relative bleeding risk about 50% but absolute risk only 0.6%.

references.authors: Schürks M, Glynn RJ, Rist PM, et al.
references.title: Effects of vitamin E on stroke subtypes: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
references.finding: Vitamin E increased hemorrhagic stroke by 22% and reduced ischemic stroke by 10%, with no effect on total stroke.

references.authors: Michaelsen MP, Poulsen M, Bjerregaard AA et al.
references.title: The Effect of Dietary Supplements on Male Infertility in Terms of Pregnancy, Live Birth, and Sperm Parameters: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: No dietary supplement improved pregnancy or live birth in infertile men; selenium, carnitine and CoQ10 improved motility and zinc+folate improved concentration, with mostly low or very-low certainty.

references.authors: Melhem SJ, Melhem M, Haddad R et al.
references.title: Pharmacologic and Nutritional Therapies in Idiopathic Male Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Antioxidants were associated with higher sperm concentration and motility, but certainty was very low, heterogeneity >80% and prediction intervals crossed the null; live-birth data were lacking.

references.authors: de Ligny W, Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility.
references.finding: Cochrane update: possible live birth increase (OR 1.43, very low certainty), no effect in low-risk-of-bias trials.

references.authors: Steiner AZ, Hansen KR, Barnhart KT, et al.
references.title: The effect of antioxidants on male factor infertility: the Males, Antioxidants, and Infertility (MOXI) randomized clinical trial.
references.finding: MOXI: a 7-ingredient antioxidant for 3-6 months did not improve semen parameters or DNA fragmentation; live birth 15% vs 24% placebo.

references.authors: Schisterman EF, Sjaarda LA, Clemons T, et al.
references.title: Effect of Folic Acid and Zinc Supplementation in Men on Semen Quality and Live Birth Among Couples Undergoing Infertility Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.n: 2370 men in couples seeking infertility care (FAZST)
references.finding: 5 mg folic acid plus 30 mg zinc for 6 months did not improve semen quality or live birth (34% vs 35%) and slightly raised sperm DNA fragmentation (+2.4 points).

references.authors: Schütz D, Lettorp KH, Olofsson IA et al.
references.title: Effect of micronutrients on fertility and aneuploidy rates in human conceptions: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: In three small trials, CoQ10 increased oocytes retrieved and live birth in poor responders (OR 2.28); in vitro, CoQ10 in maturation medium lowered aneuploidy in oocytes from older women.

references.authors: Abdelrahman MA, Gamal M, Salem SA et al.
references.title: Coenzyme Q10 Impact on Ovarian Reserve Measures and the Intra-Cytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI) Outcomes in Women with Poor Ovarian Response: A Randomized Controlled Study.
references.finding: CoQ10 before ICSI increased oocyte count, peak estradiol and embryos for transfer, but chemical and clinical pregnancy rates did not differ.

references.authors: Bakri S, Saleh R, Cayan S et al.
references.title: Efficacy and Safety of Coenzyme Q10 in Idiopathic Male Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
references.finding: CoQ10 improved sperm concentration and motility in idiopathic male infertility and reported clinical pregnancy OR 6.02, based on few small trials.

references.authors: Florou P, Anagnostis P, Theocharis P, et al.
references.title: Does coenzyme Q(10) supplementation improve fertility outcomes in women undergoing assisted reproductive technology procedures? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials.
references.finding: CoQ10 increased clinical pregnancy (28.8% vs 14.1%; OR 2.44) but not live birth (OR 1.67, NS) or miscarriage.

references.authors: Xu Y, Nisenblat V, Lu C, et al.
references.title: Pretreatment with coenzyme Q10 improves ovarian response and embryo quality in low-prognosis young women with decreased ovarian reserve: a randomized controlled trial.
references.n: 186 women <35 with poor ovarian reserve (169 analysed)
references.finding: CoQ10 600 mg/day (200 mg three times daily) for 60 days before IVF increased oocytes retrieved (median 4 vs 2), fertilization and good embryos; live birth 29% vs 16% was not statistically significant.

references.authors: ESHRE Add-ons working group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, et al.
references.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine†.
references.finding: ESHRE good practice recommendations on 42 add-ons: none based on high-quality evidence; not recommended include endometrial receptivity tests, immune testing and immunomodulators (Intralipid, IVIG), glucocorticoids, assisted hatching, time-lapse imaging (to improve live birth), intrauterine hCG, intrauterine and intraovarian PRP, mitochondrial replacement, adjuncts during stimulation (growth hormone, DHEA, testosterone), oral antioxidants and ICSI for non-male factor; PGT-A, endometrial scratching, MACS, PICSI and IMSI 'not recommended for routine clinical use'; microfluidics 'can be considered'; hyaluronan in transfer medium 'recommended' (with single embryo transfer).

references.authors: Mol BW, Bordewijk EM, Rogozińska E et al.
references.title: Data integrity of 14 randomised controlled trials.
references.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
references.finding: Integrity analysis of 14 obstetrics and gynaecology RCTs by one author found implausible baseline similarities and plagiarism; authors advise these trials not inform practice until investigated.

references.authors: Bordewijk EM, Wang R, van Wely M et al.
references.title: To share or not to share data: how valid are trials evaluating first-line ovulation induction for polycystic ovary syndrome?
references.finding: PCOS ovulation-induction trials that did not share individual data had lower quality, more statistical inconsistencies and different pooled effects than trials that did, showing how unverified small trials can bias meta-analyses.

references.authors: Ismail AM, Hamed AH, Saso S, et al.
references.title: Adding L-carnitine to clomiphene resistant PCOS women improves the quality of ovulation and the pregnancy rate. A randomized clinical trial.
references.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
references.finding: RETRACTED. Claimed L-carnitine 3 g/day with clomiphene raised pregnancy from 5.8% to 51.5%; should not be relied on.

references.authors: Ismail AM, Hamed AH, Saso S et al.
references.title: Retraction notice to "Adding l-carnitine to clomiphene resistant PCOS women improves the quality of ovulation and the pregnancy rate. A randomized clinical trial" [Eur. J. Obstet. Gynecol. Reprod. Biol. 180 (2014) 148-152].
references.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
references.finding: Retraction notice (2023) for the L-carnitine plus clomiphene PCOS RCT.

references.authors: Khaw SC, Wong ZZ, Anderson R, et al.
references.title: l-carnitine and l-acetylcarnitine supplementation for idiopathic male infertility.
references.finding: Carnitines improved total and progressive motility and morphology, with no demonstrable effect on clinical pregnancy.

references.authors: Koeth RA, Wang Z, Levison BS et al.
references.title: Intestinal microbiota metabolism of L-carnitine, a nutrient in red meat, promotes atherosclerosis.
references.finding: Gut microbes convert L-carnitine to TMAO, which accelerated atherosclerosis in mice; omnivores made more TMAO than vegans after an L-carnitine challenge.

references.authors: Dehpahni MF, Hoolari BB, Amidi F
references.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of astaxanthin efficacy in male infertility: evidence from clinical and preclinical studies.
references.finding: Pooled human trials of astaxanthin showed no significant improvement in any semen parameter versus placebo, while animal studies were strongly positive.

references.authors: Comhaire FH, El Garem Y, Mahmoud A, et al.
references.title: Combined conventional/antioxidant "Astaxanthin" treatment for male infertility: a double blind, randomized trial.
references.finding: Astaxanthin 16 mg/day for 3 months lowered seminal ROS; pregnancy 54.5% vs 10.5% in a very small trial.

references.authors: Ma B, Lu J, Kang T, et al.
references.title: Astaxanthin supplementation mildly reduced oxidative stress and inflammation biomarkers: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Astaxanthin modestly lowered blood MDA (SMD -0.95) and, in type 2 diabetes, IL-6; data on other markers were limited.

references.authors: Zhang F, Zhong Y, Li Q et al.
references.title: Does Hydrogen-Rich Water Reduce Oxidative Stress in Patients with Chronic Mountain Sickness? A Randomized, Blinded, Controlled Trial.
references.finding: Hydrogen-rich water for 8 weeks raised MDA (+2.11 vs placebo) as well as total antioxidant capacity, and did not reduce oxidative damage; more dizziness on hydrogen water.

references.authors: Todorovic N, Fernández-Landa J, Santibañez A, et al.
references.title: The Effects of Hydrogen-Rich Water on Blood Lipid Profiles in Clinical Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Hydrogen-rich water modestly lowered total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides in small clinical trials (pooled SMD about -0.2 to -0.4).

references.authors: Shen J, Zheng Y, Yu M et al.
references.title: Oral, intravenous, or sequential alpha-lipoic acid for diabetic peripheral neuropathy? A Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Network meta-analysis: the apparent superiority of sequential IV-then-oral ALA for diabetic neuropathy was a bias artefact; IV ALA was best for short-term symptoms and oral ALA for distal signs.

references.authors: Ziegler D, Low PA, Litchy WJ, et al.
references.title: Efficacy and safety of antioxidant treatment with α-lipoic acid over 4 years in diabetic polyneuropathy: the NATHAN 1 trial.
references.finding: ALA 600 mg/day for 4 years did not improve the primary composite endpoint; some secondary impairment scores improved, and serious adverse events were more frequent (38% vs 28%).

references.authors: Mijnhout GS, Kollen BJ, Alkhalaf A, et al.
references.title: Alpha lipoic Acid for symptomatic peripheral neuropathy in patients with diabetes: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: IV ALA 600 mg/day for 3 weeks clinically reduced neuropathic symptoms; the clinical relevance of 3-5 weeks of oral ALA above 600 mg/day was unclear.

references.authors: Broome SC, Whitfield J, Janssens K et al.
references.title: MitoQ supplementation does not impact redox responses to acute exercise in skeletal muscle of older individuals.
references.finding: MitoQ 20 mg/day for 12 weeks lowered muscle mitochondrial H2O2 emission capacity but did not change respiration or any exercise-induced redox signalling or gene responses.

references.authors: Snow BJ, Rolfe FL, Lockhart MM, et al.
references.title: A double-blind, placebo-controlled study to assess the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ as a disease-modifying therapy in Parkinson's disease.
references.finding: MitoQ 40 or 80 mg/day for 12 months did not slow Parkinson disease progression on any measure.

references.authors: Rossman MJ, Santos-Parker JR, Steward CAC, et al.
references.title: Chronic Supplementation With a Mitochondrial Antioxidant (MitoQ) Improves Vascular Function in Healthy Older Adults.
references.finding: MitoQ 20 mg/d for 6 weeks improved brachial flow-mediated dilation by 42% versus placebo, linked to reduced mitochondrial ROS suppression of endothelial function.

references.authors: Zhang M, Chen Y, Jiang N et al.
references.title: Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation on Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: NMN lowered diastolic blood pressure modestly (-2.15 mmHg) but not systolic overall; small trials, preliminary.

references.authors: Prokopidis K, Moriarty F, Bahat G, et al.
references.title: The Effect of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide and Riboside on Skeletal Muscle Mass and Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: NMN did not improve skeletal muscle index, grip strength, gait speed or chair-stand time; evidence does not support NMN or NR for preserving muscle in older adults.

references.authors: Harrison DE, Strong R, Reifsnyder P, et al.
references.title: 17-a-estradiol late in life extends lifespan in aging UM-HET3 male mice; nicotinamide riboside and three other drugs do not affect lifespan in either sex.
references.finding: In the NIA Interventions Testing Program, nicotinamide riboside did not extend lifespan in male or female mice.

references.authors: Yoshino M, Yoshino J, Kayser BD, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide mononucleotide increases muscle insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women.
references.finding: NMN 250 mg/day for 10 weeks increased muscle insulin sensitivity (clamp) and insulin signalling vs placebo.

references.authors: Brenner C
references.title: Comment on "Nicotinamide mononucleotide increases muscle insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women".
references.finding: Comment arguing the Yoshino NMN trial was not effectively randomized: the NMN group had far less liver fat at baseline (6.3% vs 14.8%).

references.authors: Keohane P, Everett JR, Pereira R et al.
references.title: Supplementation of spermidine at 40 mg/day has minimal effects on circulating polyamines: An exploratory double-blind randomized controlled trial in older men.
references.finding: High-purity spermidine 40 mg/day for 28 days was safe but produced no substantial change in serum or urine polyamines, indicating tight homeostatic control.

references.authors: Schwarz C, Benson GS, Horn N, et al.
references.title: Effects of Spermidine Supplementation on Cognition and Biomarkers in Older Adults With Subjective Cognitive Decline: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: Twelve months of 0.9 mg/day spermidine (wheat-germ extract) did not change memory or biomarkers vs placebo (SmartAge phase 2b).

references.authors: Kiechl S, Pechlaner R, Willeit P, et al.
references.title: Higher spermidine intake is linked to lower mortality: a prospective population-based study.
references.finding: Each 1-SD higher dietary spermidine intake was associated with 24% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.76) over 20 years; replicated in a second cohort (HR 0.71).

references.authors: Zhang N, Borné Y, Hagberg E et al.
references.title: Taurine Intake, Plasma Taurine Concentration, and Dementia Risk: Findings From the Malmö Diet and Cancer Study.
references.finding: Over 25 years, neither dietary taurine nor plasma taurine was associated with dementia, Alzheimer or vascular dementia; plasma taurine correlated only weakly with intake.

references.authors: Fernandez ME, Bernier M, Price NL, et al.
references.title: Is taurine an aging biomarker?
references.n: three human cohorts plus monkeys and mice
references.finding: Circulating taurine increased or stayed unchanged with age in three human cohorts, monkeys and mice measured longitudinally; links between taurine and health outcomes were inconsistent.

references.authors: Singh P, Gollapalli K, Mangiola S, et al.
references.title: Taurine deficiency as a driver of aging.
references.finding: Circulating taurine fell with age in mice, monkeys and humans; taurine supplementation extended mouse median lifespan and improved healthspan in mice and middle-aged monkeys; human low taurine correlated with age-related disease.

references.authors: Tzang CC, Chi LY, Lin LH, et al.
references.title: Taurine reduces the risk for metabolic syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Taurine 0.5-6 g/day lowered systolic BP by ~4 mmHg, diastolic BP by ~1.5 mmHg, fasting glucose by ~5.9 mg/dL and triglycerides by ~18 mg/dL, with no excess adverse effects.

references.authors: Faisal A, Lerche CM, Douki T et al.
references.title: Changes in ultraviolet a radiation-induced thymidine dimers and erythema after oral nicotinamide or polypodium leucotomos extract in healthy volunteers: a randomized intraindividual trial.
references.finding: Oral nicotinamide and Polypodium leucotomos each raised the UVA minimal erythema dose by 26% but neither reduced UVA-induced thymidine dimers in skin or urine.

references.authors: Middelkamp-Hup MA, Pathak MA, Parrado C, et al.
references.title: Oral Polypodium leucotomos extract decreases ultraviolet-induced damage of human skin.
references.finding: A single oral dose of Polypodium leucotomos extract (7.5 mg/kg) reduced UV erythema, sunburn cells, cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and mast-cell infiltration in irradiated skin (uncontrolled within-person design).

references.authors: Chen AC, Martin AJ, Choy B, et al.
references.title: A Phase 3 Randomized Trial of Nicotinamide for Skin-Cancer Chemoprevention.
references.finding: ONTRAC: nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily for 12 months cut new non-melanoma skin cancers by 23% (95% CI 4-38) and actinic keratoses by 11-20% versus placebo; there was no benefit after stopping.

references.authors: Allen NC, Martin AJ, Snaidr VA, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide for Skin-Cancer Chemoprevention in Transplant Recipients.
references.finding: ONTRANS: in immunosuppressed transplant recipients, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily for 12 months did not reduce keratinocyte cancers (207 vs 210; rate ratio 1.0); the trial stopped early for poor recruitment.

references.authors: Breglio KF, Knox KM, Hwang J, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide for Skin Cancer Chemoprevention.
references.finding: In Veterans Affairs records, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily was associated with 14% lower skin-cancer risk overall and 54% lower risk when started after a first skin cancer; no overall reduction was seen in transplant recipients.

references.authors: Gallagher D, Kang Y, Herrmann N et al.
references.title: Efficacy and safety of N-acetylcysteine in patients with mild cognitive impairment undergoing exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation program: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: NAC added to cardiac rehabilitation gave no cognitive benefit over placebo.

references.authors: Paschalis V, Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, et al.
references.title: N-acetylcysteine supplementation increases exercise performance and reduces oxidative stress only in individuals with low levels of glutathione.
references.finding: NAC 1,200 mg/d for 30 days restored glutathione, reduced F2-isoprostanes and improved VO2max (~14%) only in people with low baseline glutathione.

references.authors: Rizk AY, Bedaiwy MA, Al-Inany HG
references.title: N-acetyl-cysteine is a novel adjuvant to clomiphene citrate in clomiphene citrate-resistant patients with polycystic ovary syndrome.
references.finding: NAC 1.2 g/day added to clomiphene raised ovulation (49.3% vs 1.3%) and pregnancy (21.3% vs 0%) vs placebo.

references.authors: Thakker D, Raval A, Patel I, et al.
references.title: N-acetylcysteine for polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled clinical trials.
references.finding: NAC improved ovulation and pregnancy vs placebo but was inferior to metformin; trials had high risk of bias.

references.authors: Mukherjee S, Lekli I, Gurusamy N et al.
references.title: Expression of the longevity proteins by both red and white wines and their cardioprotective components, resveratrol, tyrosol, and hydroxytyrosol.
references.finding: RETRACTED: one of several Dipak Das laboratory papers on resveratrol and wine cardioprotection retracted after a research-misconduct investigation.

references.authors: Dudley J, Das S, Mukherjee S et al.
references.title: Resveratrol, a unique phytoalexin present in red wine, delivers either survival signal or death signal to the ischemic myocardium depending on dose.
references.finding: RETRACTED: Das laboratory paper on dose-dependent resveratrol effects in ischaemic myocardium, retracted after a research-misconduct investigation.

references.authors: Nelson KM, Dahlin JL, Bisson J, et al.
references.title: The Essential Medicinal Chemistry of Curcumin.
references.finding: Argues curcumin is a PAINS/IMPS compound that is chemically unstable, reactive and not bioavailable; states that no double-blind placebo-controlled curcumin trial had been successful as of 2017.

references.authors: Chen J, Zhou Q, Yu W, et al.
references.title: A critical review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of curcumin for knee osteoarthritis.
references.finding: Overview of curcumin-for-knee-OA reviews: methodological quality extremely low, heavy overlap, and 37 of 48 outcomes rated extremely low-quality evidence.

references.authors: Dehzad MJ, Ghalandari H, Nouri M, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of curcumin/turmeric supplementation in adults: A GRADE-assessed systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Turmeric/curcumin lowered CRP (-0.58 mg/L), TNF-a and IL-6 (-1.31 pg/mL), raised TAC (+0.21 mmol/L) and SOD, and lowered MDA (-0.33 umol/L); IL-1b unchanged.

references.authors: Wang Z, Singh A, Jones G, et al.
references.title: Efficacy and Safety of Turmeric Extracts for the Treatment of Knee Osteoarthritis: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Turmeric extracts reduced knee OA pain (SMD -0.82) and improved function versus placebo, similar to NSAIDs; very high heterogeneity, moderate risk of bias, less benefit with higher BMI.

references.authors: Kocher A, Bohnert L, Schiborr C, et al.
references.title: Highly bioavailable micellar curcuminoids accumulate in blood, are safe and do not reduce blood lipids and inflammation markers in moderately hyperlipidemic individuals.
references.finding: 294 mg/day micellar curcuminoids for 6 weeks reached fasting plasma ~49 nmol/L but did not change lipids, CRP or other inflammation markers versus placebo.

references.authors: Du J, Liu J, Liu Q et al.
references.title: Efficacy and safety of nutritional supplements in female infertility: a network meta-analysis.
references.finding: Network meta-analysis ranked curcumin, astaxanthin and vitamin D combinations highest for oocyte and pregnancy outcomes, but almost all comparisons were low or very-low certainty.

references.authors: Clifford T, Jeffries O, Stevenson EJ, et al.
references.title: The effects of vitamin C and E on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: a systematic review and Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Across 9 aerobic and 9 resistance-training RCTs, vitamin C and/or E did not significantly attenuate gains in VO2max, endurance performance, lean mass or strength; trials were small.

references.authors: Ristow M, Zarse K, Oberbach A, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants prevent health-promoting effects of physical exercise in humans.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Vitamin C 1,000 mg/d plus vitamin E 400 IU/d during 4 weeks of exercise training abolished the training-induced gains in insulin sensitivity and endogenous antioxidant gene expression.

references.authors: Martinez-Negrin G, Acton JP, Cocksedge SP, et al.
references.title: The effect of dietary (poly)phenols on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: A systematic review and meta-analysis of human intervention trials.
references.finding: (Poly)phenols did not change training gains in strength, power or VO2max; isoflavones may add lean mass while resveratrol tended to impair adaptations (SMD -0.54, NS).

references.authors: Tavenier J, Berglind M, Hach LF et al.
references.title: Low-Dose Fisetin Supplementation and Its Association With Chronic Inflammation in Middle-Aged and Older Adults: Study Protocol for a Triple-Blind, Randomised, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
references.finding: Protocol (2026) for a triple-blind RCT of 100 mg/day fisetin on suPAR in adults aged 50+; human efficacy data are still pending.

references.authors: Harrison DE, Strong R, Reifsnyder P, et al.
references.title: Astaxanthin and meclizine extend lifespan in UM-HET3 male mice; fisetin, SG1002 (hydrogen sulfide donor), dimethyl fumarate, mycophenolic acid, and 4-phenylbutyrate do not significantly affect lifespan in either sex at the doses and schedules used.
references.finding: In the NIA Interventions Testing Program, astaxanthin extended median male mouse lifespan by 12%, with no significant effect in females or on 90th-percentile lifespan.

references.authors: Yousefzadeh MJ, Zhu Y, McGowan SJ, et al.
references.title: Fisetin is a senotherapeutic that extends health and lifespan.
references.finding: Fisetin was the most potent senolytic of 10 flavonoids screened; late-life dosing reduced senescence markers and extended median and maximum lifespan in mice.

references.authors: Lizzo G, Migliavacca E, Lamers D, et al.
references.title: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial in Healthy Older Adults to Determine Efficacy of Glycine and N-Acetylcysteine Supplementation on Glutathione Redox Status and Oxidative Damage.
references.finding: Industry-run RCT: GlyNAC at 2.4, 4.8 or 7.2 g/day for 2 weeks did not raise glutathione or the GSH:GSSG ratio (primary endpoint); a post-hoc subgroup with high oxidative stress and low glutathione responded.

references.authors: Kumar P, Liu C, Suliburk J, et al.
references.title: Supplementing Glycine and N-Acetylcysteine (GlyNAC) in Older Adults Improves Glutathione Deficiency, Oxidative Stress, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, Inflammation, Physical Function, and Aging Hallmarks: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: In a placebo-controlled 16-week RCT, GlyNAC improved glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, insulin resistance and physical function in older adults.

references.authors: Smith E, Ottosson F, Hellstrand S, et al.
references.title: Ergothioneine is associated with reduced mortality and decreased risk of cardiovascular disease.
references.finding: Higher plasma ergothioneine was associated with lower coronary disease (HR 0.85/SD), cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.79) and overall mortality (HR 0.86) over 21 years.

references.authors: Ba DM, Gao X, Al-Shaar L, et al.
references.title: Prospective study of dietary mushroom intake and risk of mortality: results from continuous National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2003-2014 and a meta-analysis.
references.finding: Mushroom intake was associated with slightly lower all-cause mortality (pooled RR 0.94) in cohort studies; the NHANES analysis alone was non-significant.

references.authors: Miller RA, Harrison DE, Astle CM, et al.
references.title: Glycine supplementation extends lifespan of male and female mice.
references.finding: In the NIA Interventions Testing Program, an 8% glycine diet extended lifespan of male and female genetically heterogeneous mice by 4-6%.

references.authors: Bannai M, Kawai N, Ono K, et al.
references.title: The effects of glycine on subjective daytime performance in partially sleep-restricted healthy volunteers.
references.finding: 3 g glycine before bed during 3 nights of 25% sleep restriction reduced daytime fatigue and improved psychomotor vigilance compared with placebo.

references.authors: Valenzuela PL, Morales JS, Castillo-García A, et al.
references.title: Acute Ketone Supplementation and Exercise Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Acute ketone supplements (esters or salts) had no effect on exercise performance (Hedges g = -0.05) from sprints to ~50-min events.

references.authors: Bonnechère B, Stephens EB, Boileau AC, et al.
references.title: The effect of exogenous ketone bodies on cognition across health and disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Exogenous ketones produced a small improvement in cognitive performance vs placebo (SMD 0.29) across healthy and clinical groups.

references.authors: Albert BB, Derraik JG, Cameron-Smith D, et al.
references.title: Fish oil supplements in New Zealand are highly oxidised and do not meet label content of n-3 PUFA.
references.finding: Of 32 New Zealand fish-oil supplements, 83% exceeded the recommended peroxide value, 25% anisidine value and 50% TOTOX; only 8% met all limits and most contained <67% of labelled EPA+DHA.

references.authors: Bannenberg G, Mallon C, Edwards H, et al.
references.title: Omega-3 Long-Chain Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid Content and Oxidation State of Fish Oil Supplements in New Zealand.
references.finding: Industry-association (GOED) testing of 47 New Zealand fish-oil products found 72-86% compliant with voluntary oxidation limits and 91% meeting EPA/DHA label claims, contradicting Albert 2015.

references.authors: Ottestad I, Vogt G, Retterstøl K, et al.
references.title: Oxidised fish oil does not influence established markers of oxidative stress in healthy human subjects: a randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: 7 weeks of 8 g/day oxidized fish oil (1.6 g EPA+DHA) did not change urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha, plasma HNE/HHE, hs-CRP or antioxidant enzymes vs fresh fish oil or high-oleic sunflower oil.

references.authors: Rundblad A, Holven KB, Ottestad I, et al.
references.title: High-quality fish oil has a more favourable effect than oxidised fish oil on intermediate-density lipoprotein and LDL subclasses: a randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: High-quality fish oil (PV 4) lowered IDL and LDL particle subclasses compared with oxidized fish oil (PV 18, AV 9) and high-oleic sunflower oil.

references.authors: Manach C, Williamson G, Morand C, et al.
references.title: Bioavailability and bioefficacy of polyphenols in humans. I. Review of 97 bioavailability studies.
references.finding: After 50 mg aglycone equivalents, plasma polyphenol metabolites reach only 0-4 umol/L and urinary excretion is 0.3-43% of dose, varying greatly by compound.

references.authors: Halliwell B
references.title: Are polyphenols antioxidants or pro-oxidants? What do we learn from cell culture and in vivo studies?
references.finding: Neither antioxidant nor pro-oxidant effects of polyphenols are established in humans at achievable levels; many cell-culture results are artefacts of polyphenol oxidation in media.

references.authors: Aebi S, Assereto R, Lauterburg BH
references.title: High-dose intravenous glutathione in man. Pharmacokinetics and effects on cyst(e)ine in plasma and urine.
references.finding: Intravenous glutathione (2 g/m2) had a plasma half-life of about 14 minutes and was rapidly broken down or excreted in urine.

references.authors: Richie JP Jr, Nichenametla S, Neidig W, et al.
references.title: Randomized controlled trial of oral glutathione supplementation on body stores of glutathione.
references.finding: Oral glutathione 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months raised blood glutathione stores by 17-35%, which returned to baseline after a 1-month washout.

references.authors: Thomson CA, Chow HHS, Wertheim BC, et al.
references.title: A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of diindolylmethane for breast cancer biomarker modulation in patients taking tamoxifen.
references.finding: DIM 150 mg twice daily for 12 months raised the 2/16 ratio and SHBG but lowered plasma tamoxifen metabolites including endoxifen; breast density was unchanged.

references.authors: National Toxicology Program
references.title: Toxicology studies of indole-3-carbinol in F344/N rats and B6C3F1/N mice and toxicology and carcinogenesis studies of indole-3-carbinol in Harlan Sprague Dawley rats and B6C3F1/N mice (gavage studies).
references.journal: Natl Toxicol Program Tech Rep Ser
references.finding: Two-year gavage studies found clear evidence of carcinogenicity of indole-3-carbinol (liver tumours) in male mice and some evidence (uterine adenocarcinoma) in female rats; none in male rats or female mice.

references.authors: Serban MC, Sahebkar A, Zanchetti A, et al.
references.title: Effects of Quercetin on Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Quercetin lowered blood pressure by ~3.0/2.6 mmHg overall; the effect was confined to doses of 500 mg/day or more (-4.5/-3.0 mmHg).

references.authors: Heinz SA, Henson DA, Austin MD, et al.
references.title: Quercetin supplementation and upper respiratory tract infection: A randomized community clinical trial.
references.finding: 500 or 1000 mg/day quercetin for 12 weeks did not reduce upper respiratory infections overall; a post-hoc subgroup of fit adults aged 40+ had 31-36% fewer sick days and lower severity on 1000 mg.

references.authors: Zeraattalab-Motlagh S, Jayedi A, Shab-Bidar S
references.title: The effects of resveratrol supplementation in patients with type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease: an umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Resveratrol effects in type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome and fatty liver were trivial or of very low certainty; the evidence does not support supplementation (short-term HbA1c the exception).

references.authors: Gliemann L, Schmidt JF, Olesen J, et al.
references.title: Resveratrol blunts the positive effects of exercise training on cardiovascular health in aged men.
references.finding: 250 mg/day resveratrol during 8 weeks of high-intensity training cut the VO2max gain by 45% and abolished training-induced improvements in blood pressure, LDL and triglycerides.

references.authors: Ochiai A, Kuroda K, Ikemoto Y, et al.
references.title: Influence of resveratrol supplementation on IVF-embryo transfer cycle outcomes.
references.finding: Resveratrol 200 mg/day during embryo-transfer cycles was associated with lower clinical pregnancy (OR 0.54) and higher miscarriage (OR 2.60).

references.authors: Wilson CP, McNulty H, Ward M, et al.
references.title: Blood pressure in treated hypertensive individuals with the MTHFR 677TT genotype is responsive to intervention with riboflavin: findings of a targeted randomized trial.
references.finding: 1.6 mg/day riboflavin for 16 weeks lowered systolic BP by 5.6 mmHg vs placebo in this genotype.

references.authors: Stranges S, Marshall JR, Natarajan R, et al.
references.title: Effects of long-term selenium supplementation on the incidence of type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial.
references.finding: Selenium 200 ug/d increased type 2 diabetes incidence (HR 1.55), especially in the top tertile of baseline selenium (HR 2.70).

references.authors: Rayman MP, Winther KH, Pastor-Barriuso R, et al.
references.title: Effect of long-term selenium supplementation on mortality: Results from a multiple-dose, randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: 300 ug/day selenium for 5 years raised all-cause mortality over 10 years (HR 1.59, 1.02-2.46); 100 and 200 ug showed no harm.

references.authors: Vinceti M, Filippini T, Del Giovane C, et al.
references.title: Selenium for preventing cancer.
references.finding: High-certainty evidence that selenium supplementation does not reduce cancer incidence (RR 1.01) or cancer mortality.

references.authors: Safarinejad MR, Safarinejad S
references.title: Expression of Concern: Efficacy of Selenium and/or N-Acetyl-Cysteine for Improving Semen Parameters in Infertile Men: A Double-Blind, Placebo Controlled, Randomized Study.
references.finding: Journal of Urology Expression of Concern regarding the Safarinejad selenium/NAC trial.

references.authors: Safarinejad MR, Safarinejad S
references.title: Efficacy of selenium and/or N-acetyl-cysteine for improving semen parameters in infertile men: a double-blind, placebo controlled, randomized study.
references.finding: Reported that 200 ug selenium and/or 600 mg NAC improved all semen parameters; the journal issued an Expression of Concern in 2023.

references.authors: Saito A, Ishikawa S, Yang K, et al.
references.title: Sulforaphane as a potential therapeutic agent: a comprehensive analysis of clinical trials and mechanistic insights.
references.finding: Of 84 registered sulforaphane/broccoli-extract trials only 39 were published, raising publication-bias concerns; summarises effects by disease category.

references.authors: Wise RA, Holbrook JT, Criner G, et al.
references.title: Lack of Effect of Oral Sulforaphane Administration on Nrf2 Expression in COPD: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo Controlled Trial.
references.finding: 25 or 150 µmol/day sulforaphane for 4 weeks was absorbed but did not induce Nrf2 target genes in lung cells or change oxidative stress or inflammation markers.

references.authors: Axelsson AS, Tubbs E, Mecham B, et al.
references.title: Sulforaphane reduces hepatic glucose production and improves glucose control in patients with type 2 diabetes.
references.finding: Broccoli sprout extract (150 µmol sulforaphane/day, 12 weeks) reduced fasting blood glucose and HbA1c in obese patients with dysregulated type 2 diabetes (not in the whole group); in cells and animals sulforaphane suppressed hepatic gluconeogenesis via NRF2.

references.authors: Liu S, D'Amico D, Shankland E, et al.
references.title: Effect of Urolithin A Supplementation on Muscle Endurance and Mitochondrial Health in Older Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: 1000 mg/day urolithin A for 4 months improved hand and leg muscle endurance and lowered CRP and acylcarnitines, but the primary endpoints (6-minute walk, maximal ATP production) did not differ from placebo.

references.authors: Singh A, D'Amico D, Andreux PA, et al.
references.title: Urolithin A improves muscle strength, exercise performance, and biomarkers of mitochondrial health in a randomized trial in middle-aged adults.
references.finding: 500-1000 mg/day urolithin A for 4 months raised muscle strength ~12% and improved VO2peak and 6-minute walk, but not the primary endpoint (peak power output); company-sponsored.

references.authors: Whitfield J, McKay AKA, Tee N, et al.
references.title: Evaluating the Impact of Urolithin A Supplementation on Running Performance, Recovery, and Mitochondrial Biomarkers in Highly Trained Male Distance Runners.
