audit.claim: Vitamin D-replete women have about 33% higher odds of IVF live birth than deficient women, RCTs show only a chemical-pregnancy gain, so test and correct deficiency before IVF (general impact 2); in men high-dose vitamin D did not improve semen.
audit.biases: The IVF association [anut-chu2018] is observational and exposed to reverse causation and confounding: low 25(OH)D tracks obesity, inactivity, less time outdoors, inflammation and chronic illness, and a systematic review of 290 cohorts and 172 trials concluded low 25(OH)D is mainly a marker of ill health because trials did not reproduce cohort associations even in people starting below 50 nmol/L [anut-autier2014]; a letter questioned whether the IVF association had been demonstrated at all [anut-iliuta2018]. Causal genetic evidence is weaker than it looked: the 2021 non-linear Mendelian randomization paper suggesting deficiency causally raised mortality was retracted and republished in 2024 with null results at every 25(OH)D level [anut-sofianopoulou2021, anut-erfc2024], because the residual stratification method is biased when the genetic effect on 25(OH)D varies [anut-burgess2023]; a similar 2022 analysis using the same method [anut-sutherland2022] carries the same caveat.
audit.newer_evidence: Fertility: a 2021 double-blind RCT in 630 women with 25(OH)D below 30 ng/mL found a 600,000 IU dose did not raise clinical pregnancy (RR 0.91) in any subgroup [anut-somigliana2021], and a 2026 BMJ multicentre RCT of 876 women with PCOS and mean 25(OH)D of 16 ng/mL found 4000 IU/day before IVF doubled 25(OH)D but left live birth unchanged (52.0% vs 50.2%; RR 1.03) [anut-hu2026]; these supersede the small 2022 trial-sequential meta-analysis [anut-zhou2022]. Male: the 330-man RCT remains null for semen quality [anut-blomberg2018]. General health: VITAL (2019) [anut-manson2019], D-Health (2022 mortality HR 1.04; 2023 CVD HR 0.91, borderline) [anut-neale2022, anut-thompson2023] and DO-HEALTH (2020) [anut-bischoffferrari2020] were null on primary outcomes. The Endocrine Society (2024) now suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing and against supplementing above the DRI in healthy adults under 75 [anut-demay2024]. On the other side, 2026 UK Biobank target-trial emulations argue the big trials enrolled mostly replete people and predict real benefit in deficient people [anut-wang2026a, anut-wang2026b], but these rely on the same observational associations that trials and corrected MR have not confirmed.
audit.bottom_line: Correcting true deficiency is reasonable for bone and general health, but there is now good randomized evidence that vitamin D does not raise IVF live birth, even in women with low levels; the observational IVF link is probably confounding.

site_change.headline: Low vitamin D is linked to poorer IVF results in cohort studies, but randomized trials in deficient women (630 and 876 women) found supplementation did not raise pregnancy or live birth (52% vs 50%), so the link is probably confounding by overall health.
site_change.note: Replace 'Test 25(OH)D and correct deficiency' framing with 'correct known deficiency for general health; not an IVF treatment', and note the Endocrine Society 2024 advice against routine testing. Fill the empty debate field with the cohort-vs-RCT and retracted-MR points. Cite the retracted Sofianopoulou 2021 paper only as retracted.

audit.claim: No cardiovascular or cancer benefit in more than 100,000 trial participants; 400 IU/day raised prostate cancer 17% and haemorrhagic stroke, and high doses slightly raise mortality.
audit.biases: The original belief in vitamin E came from cohorts where supplement users were healthier (healthy-user bias); RCTs reversed it [anut-hope2000, anut-lee2005, anut-sesso2008, anut-klein2011]. The mortality part of the claim rests on trial-level meta-analysis [anut-miller2005, anut-bjelakovic2012], which is sensitive to which trials are pooled and how doses are modelled.
audit.newer_evidence: The no-benefit and prostate-cancer findings hold [anut-klein2011], and USPSTF kept a grade D recommendation in 2022 [anut-uspstf2022]. Haemorrhagic stroke harm is supported by a 9-trial meta-analysis (RR 1.22) [anut-schurks2010]. The mortality signal is contested: a Bayesian re-analysis concluded vitamin E is unlikely to affect mortality at any dose [anut-berry2009], and a 57-trial meta-analysis with 246,371 people found RR 1.00 with no dose-response [anut-abner2011]. Proponents argue the trials were flawed because doses did not lower oxidative stress [anut-blumberg2007], but the dose needed (1600 IU/day or more) is itself a bleeding-risk dose. Mendelian randomization found no protective effect of genetically higher tocopherols on coronary disease [anut-luo2021].
audit.bottom_line: Vitamin E pills do not prevent heart disease or cancer and raise prostate cancer and haemorrhagic stroke risk; whether they raise overall mortality is genuinely disputed and probably small at most.

site_change.headline: No cardiovascular or cancer benefit in more than 100,000 trial participants; 400 IU/day raised prostate cancer by 17% and haemorrhagic stroke by 22%; meta-analyses disagree on whether high doses slightly raise overall mortality.
site_change.note: Fill the empty debate field: Miller 2005 and Bjelakovic 2012 (mortality harm) versus Berry 2009 and Abner 2011 (no mortality effect), and the 'trials used too-low doses' argument.

audit.claim: 20-30 mg/day beta-carotene raised lung cancer 18-28% and mortality 8-17% in smokers and asbestos workers; no benefit for anyone; USPSTF recommends against it.
audit.biases: This is the textbook case of an observational association reversed by trials: high blood beta-carotene marked a fruit- and vegetable-rich, non-smoking lifestyle (residual confounding by diet and smoking), and supplements caused harm [anut-atbc1994, anut-omenn1996].
audit.newer_evidence: Post-trial follow-ups show the excess lung cancer faded after stopping in ATBC (18-year RR 1.04) [anut-virtamo2014] but persisted, non-significantly, in CARET, especially in women (RR 1.12) [anut-goodman2004]. A 2021 Mendelian randomization of 768,121 people found genetically higher beta-carotene had no effect on coronary disease (OR 1.03) [anut-luo2021], consistent with the null HPS trial. USPSTF reaffirmed grade D in 2022 [anut-uspstf2022].
audit.bottom_line: Still correct: beta-carotene supplements help nobody and harm smokers; the risk appears to fade some years after stopping.

site_change.note: Add the post-trial follow-ups (ATBC harm faded; CARET excess persisted in women) to timeframe or caveats, and the MR null for coronary disease to the empty debate field.

audit.claim: No effect on cardiovascular disease, cancer or mortality in large RCTs; shortens colds about 8%; about 1 g/day doubles kidney-stone risk in men; megadoses need IV dosing.
audit.biases: The kidney-stone figure (RR 1.95) is from one Swedish cohort [anut-thomas2013], open to confounding by who takes high-dose supplements and to self-report error. The outcome-null findings are from RCTs [anut-sesso2008] and the cold data from a Cochrane review [anut-hemila2013].
audit.newer_evidence: A larger US analysis of three cohorts replicated a smaller kidney-stone association in men only (HR 1.19 for 1000 mg/day or more supplemental; none in women) [anut-ferraro2016]. Mendelian randomization found genetically higher plasma ascorbate did not lower coronary disease [anut-luo2021]. The IV megadose route has now been tested in a large RCT: in sepsis, IV vitamin C increased death or persistent organ dysfunction (RR 1.21) [anut-lamontagne2022].
audit.bottom_line: Oral vitamin C beyond what food provides does not prevent chronic disease; high doses carry a modest kidney-stone risk in men, and IV megadoses are not harmless.

site_change.note: Present the kidney-stone risk as observational and as a range (HR about 1.2 in the larger US cohorts to RR 1.95 in the Swedish cohort), and add LOVIT to notes on IV dosing so 'pharmacological levels need IV dosing' is not read as a recommendation.

audit.claim: An uncontrolled study found 1 g C + 1 g E lowered sperm DNA fragmentation and boosted the next ICSI pregnancy rate, but controlled trials of similar mixes are null; no RCT shows more live births in women.
audit.biases: Greco 2005 is a before-after design after a failed cycle, so regression to the mean drives much of the effect [anut-greco2005]. Female data rest on a Cochrane review that included trials later retracted [anut-showell2020].
audit.newer_evidence: MOXI found no semen or DNA-fragmentation benefit and numerically fewer live births (15% vs 24%) [anut-steiner2020]; Cochrane 2022 found no effect in low-risk-of-bias trials [anut-deligny2022]; a 2025 meta-analysis of 50 studies found no supplement improved pregnancy or live birth [anut-michaelsen2025].
audit.bottom_line: Controlled trials don't support high-dose vitamin C and E for men with high DNA fragmentation before ICSI.

site_change.note: Soften dose.effective ('If used before ICSI for high SDF: 500-1000 mg C + 400 IU E') to 'not supported by controlled trials', and add the 2025 meta-analysis.

audit.claim: Selenium follows a U-curve: benefit only in deficiency; in replete people 200 ug/day raised type 2 diabetes (HR 1.55) and 300 ug/day raised 10-year mortality; no cancer prevention; the main positive male-fertility trial carries an Expression of Concern.
audit.biases: Mostly RCT-based [anut-stranges2007, anut-vinceti2018]; the high-grade prostate cancer finding is a case-cohort subgroup by baseline status [anut-kristal2014], and the 300 ug mortality result has a wide CI (1.02-2.46) [anut-rayman2018].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer trial overturns this. The integrity concern stands: the Safarinejad selenium/NAC trial has a 2023 Expression of Concern [anut-safarinejad2009, anut-jurol2023]. Newer male-infertility meta-analyses find selenium improves motility but not pregnancy or live birth, at low certainty [anut-michaelsen2025, anut-deligny2022].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged: supplement selenium only for low intake or status; in replete people it adds risk without benefit.

audit.claim: Across 78 RCTs antioxidant supplements did not lower mortality and slightly raised it in low-bias trials (RR 1.04); HPS found nothing; they blunt training; high doses may loosen sperm chromatin.
audit.biases: The pooled mortality RR depends on trial selection; the vitamin E component is disputed [anut-abner2011, anut-berry2009]. The sperm harm rests on an uncontrolled study and mice [anut-menezo2007, anut-moazamian2025].
audit.newer_evidence: Mendelian randomization of 768,121 people found genetically higher circulating antioxidants (retinol, carotenoids, ascorbate, tocopherols) did not lower coronary disease [anut-luo2021], supporting 'no benefit' independent of trial selection. Mouse work extended the tumour concern from progression to metastasis via BACH1 [anut-wiel2019]. For sperm, MOXI [anut-steiner2020] and a 2025 meta-analysis [anut-michaelsen2025] found no live-birth benefit, while a 2026 meta-analysis found semen-parameter gains of very low certainty [anut-melhem2026].
audit.bottom_line: No benefit is well established; a small mortality harm is likely for beta-carotene and possible but disputed for the mix as a whole.

site_change.note: Fill the empty debate field with Bjelakovic 2012 vs Abner 2011/Berry 2009 on mortality, and add the 2021 MR null.

audit.claim: Gram-level vitamin C + E and 150-250 mg resveratrol blunted molecular and some functional training adaptations in several RCTs, although meta-analyses find no significant loss of VO2max, endurance or strength.
audit.biases: Small trials (11-54 people), many outcomes and selective emphasis on molecular markers inflate apparent blunting; trials on both sides are cited [anut-ristow2009, anut-clifford2020].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 RCT found 12 weeks of the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ did not alter exercise-induced redox signalling or gene responses in older muscle [anut-broome2025], showing that not every antioxidant blunts signalling. Polyphenol meta-analysis still shows a non-significant tendency for resveratrol to impair adaptation [anut-martineznegrin2022].
audit.bottom_line: The balanced claim holds: chronic gram doses are not useful during training and may blunt adaptation, but performance loss is not proven.

audit.claim: Vitamin E during radiotherapy nearly tripled second cancers (HR 2.88) and antioxidant use during breast chemotherapy was linked to more recurrence (HR 1.41); default is no high-dose antioxidants during treatment without the oncology team.
audit.biases: The breast-cancer HR is observational (self-reported use, confounding by indication and by who chooses supplements) and borderline (CI 0.98-2.04) [anut-ambrosone2020]. The radiotherapy result is an RCT but in head-and-neck patients, mostly smokers [anut-bairati2005].
audit.newer_evidence: No large RCT has settled the question. Mechanistic work strengthened the plausibility: NAC and vitamin E accelerated lung-tumour progression [anut-sayin2014] and promoted metastasis via BACH1 in mice [anut-wiel2019]. The precautionary default is reasonable.
audit.bottom_line: Still sound advice; the human evidence is one RCT plus observational data, backed by consistent animal data.

audit.claim: PHS II (cancer HR 0.92) and COSMOS (HR 0.97) disagree on cancer, neither cut heart disease or death, a 390,000-person cohort found no mortality benefit, COSMOS slowed cognitive ageing 0.07 SD; multivitamin users had 41% less ovulatory infertility.
audit.biases: Multivitamin cohorts are the classic healthy-user setting: users eat better, smoke less and see doctors more, so older cohort benefits were inflated; the 2024 three-cohort analysis found no mortality benefit despite this [anut-loftfield2024]. The ovulatory-infertility RR 0.59 [anut-chavarro2008] comes from the same kind of cohort and has no RCT behind it. The cognitive result comes from one trial programme with several sub-studies by overlapping investigators.
audit.newer_evidence: Cognition: COSMOS-Mind (0.07 SD global cognition) [anut-baker2023] and the online COSMOS-Web substudy (better word recall) [anut-yeung2023] were pooled with the clinic substudy [anut-vyas2024]; all are COSMOS, so independent replication is still lacking, and PHS II found no cognitive effect [anut-gaziano2012]. Cancer/CVD: COSMOS null [anut-sesso2022]; USPSTF 2022 insufficient evidence [anut-uspstf2022].
audit.bottom_line: A standard multivitamin is reasonable insurance for shortfalls with a small, COSMOS-only cognitive signal; it is not a fertility treatment.

site_change.note: Label the ovulatory-infertility RR 0.59 as observational and prone to healthy-user bias (it currently sits beside RCT numbers in key_numbers without a qualifier), and note the cognitive benefit comes from one trial programme.

audit.claim: In MCI with high homocysteine, folic acid + B6 + B12 slowed brain atrophy about 30% (53% if homocysteine >13 umol/L) in VITACOG, while 11 trials in ~22,000 people showed no effect on cognitive ageing.
audit.biases: The strongest effects are subgroup and post hoc findings from one 168-person MRI trial [anut-smith2010]; brain atrophy is a surrogate. The homocysteine-dementia link comes largely from cohorts, where homocysteine also marks kidney function, B12 status, smoking and vascular disease (residual confounding).
audit.newer_evidence: Mendelian randomization tested the causal chain directly: genetically predicted homocysteine, serum folate and vitamin B12 were not associated with Alzheimer disease [anut-larsson2017], which undercuts the premise that lowering homocysteine prevents dementia. The 11-trial meta-analysis remains null [anut-clarke2014], although proponents dispute it [anut-garrard2015, anut-smith2018].
audit.bottom_line: B vitamins correct deficiency and lower homocysteine, but causal evidence that this protects cognition is weak; treat VITACOG as a hypothesis for high-homocysteine MCI.

site_change.note: Add the Larsson 2017 MR null to the debate field; keep impact 1 and evidence limited.

audit.claim: FAZST (2370 couples) found folic acid + zinc did nothing for semen or live birth and slightly raised DNA fragmentation.
audit.biases: Large, well-run RCT with live birth as outcome [anut-schisterman2020]; population not selected for deficiency.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of 50 studies found no supplement, including zinc and folate, improved pregnancy or live birth in men [anut-michaelsen2025].
audit.bottom_line: Still the best-quality null result in male fertility supplements.

audit.claim: Zinc supplements do little in replete people (FAZST null), 50 mg/day already depresses copper-dependent SOD1, and 100+ mg/day causes copper-deficiency anaemia and myelopathy.
audit.biases: Low seminal zinc in infertile men [anut-zhao2016] is cross-sectional and may reflect, not cause, poor semen; the anti-inflammatory meta-analysis is heterogeneous and was criticised [anut-hosseini2021, anut-jafari2021].
audit.newer_evidence: FAZST [anut-schisterman2020] and the 2025 meta-analysis [anut-michaelsen2025] show no live-birth benefit; copper harm at high zinc is long established [anut-fischer1984].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

audit.claim: Iron pills without deficiency raise faecal free-radical production and, in infant trials, shift gut bacteria toward pathogens; genetic studies link lifelong higher iron to shorter lifespan and more diabetes.
audit.biases: Adult evidence is mostly mechanistic or genetic; MR on serum iron [anut-daghlas2021] estimates lifelong exposure and may involve pleiotropy of iron-regulating variants, so it does not directly quantify the effect of a few years of supplements.
audit.newer_evidence: A natural experiment supports the genetic arm: HFE C282Y homozygotes (lifelong iron loading) in UK Biobank had more liver disease, arthritis and diabetes (OR 1.53 in men) and more incident morbidity [anut-pilling2019]. Against over-generalising, iron in iron-replete pregnancy still reduced anaemia and low birthweight [anut-hansen2023].
audit.bottom_line: Iron the body does not need is not harmless, but the clearest harm is from genetic overload; at multivitamin doses adult harm is unproven.

site_change.note: Add the HFE C282Y cohort as supporting genetic evidence and state that it reflects overload, not typical supplement doses.

audit.claim: EFSA (2018): 800 mg EGCG/day or more from supplements significantly raises liver transaminases; extracts also cause rare severe liver injury.
audit.biases: Case series are subject to reporting bias, but the threshold is from RCTs [anut-efsa2018].
audit.newer_evidence: The largest RCT behind the threshold, the Minnesota Green Tea Trial (1075 women, 843 mg EGCG/day for a year), raised ALT in 6.7% vs 0.7% on placebo, with 1.3% serious ALT events [anut-dostal2015]; a 2023 analysis linked a UGT1A4 genotype to much larger ALT rises [anut-acosta2023].
audit.bottom_line: Holds, with a concrete trial number readers can use: about 1 in 15 women on 843 mg/day EGCG developed raised ALT.

site_change.note: Add the MGTT figures (6.7% vs 0.7% ALT elevation; 1.3% serious) to key_numbers and fill the debate field (genetic susceptibility; brewed tea safe).

audit.claim: Vitamin E raised haemorrhagic stroke 22%, NAC with nitroglycerin caused hypotension and headache, St John's wort speeds contraceptive breakdown; fish oil did not raise bleeding overall in 120,643 trial patients, with a small signal for high-dose purified EPA.
audit.biases: The fish-oil bleeding signal comes mainly from REDUCE-IT, whose mineral-oil placebo raised LDL, hs-CRP (+21.9%) and IL-1beta in the control arm [anut-ridker2022], which may distort comparisons; STRENGTH, with a corn-oil placebo, found no cardiovascular benefit [anut-nicholls2020].
audit.newer_evidence: An often-missed omega-3 harm: a 2021 meta-analysis of 7 cardiovascular RCTs (81,210 patients) found marine omega-3 supplements raised atrial fibrillation (HR 1.25; 1.49 above 1 g/day; +11% per extra gram) [anut-gencer2021]; REDUCE-IT also had more AF hospitalisation (3.1% vs 2.1%) and borderline more serious bleeding (2.7% vs 2.1%) [anut-bhatt2019]. The bleeding meta-analysis remains reassuring overall [anut-javaid2024]; vitamin E stroke data are unchanged [anut-schurks2010].
audit.bottom_line: Add atrial fibrillation: people with AF risk, or on anticoagulants for AF, should discuss gram-dose fish oil with their prescriber.

site_change.note: Add the dose-related AF risk of omega-3 supplements (HR 1.25; 1.49 above 1 g/day) and the REDUCE-IT mineral-oil placebo caveat to the fish-oil part of the debate.

audit.claim: Independent surveys found 50-83% of fish-oil supplements over oxidation limits (industry survey: most compliant); 7 weeks of oxidized oil did not raise isoprostanes but lost the LDL benefit.
audit.biases: Both sides of the survey dispute have commercial affiliations [anut-albert2015, anut-bannenberg2017]; human trials are short and small [anut-ottestad2012, anut-rundblad2017].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer human outcome trial of oxidized oil was found. Large omega-3 outcome trials raise a separate dose-related atrial fibrillation risk regardless of oxidation [anut-gencer2021].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged and fairly stated.

audit.claim: Egg: 600 mg/day for 60 days before IVF increased eggs and good embryos in young poor responders and meta-analyses show higher clinical pregnancy (OR ~2.2-2.4) but no significant live-birth gain. Sperm: modest motility gains, no pregnancy evidence.
audit.biases: Small, often open-label single-centre trials (Xu 2018 excluded non-compliant women) [anut-xu2018]; such fertility-supplement trials are prone to integrity problems, as shown for PCOS ovulation-induction trials that did not share data [anut-bordewijk2020] and for one author's 14 RCTs [anut-mol2024].
audit.newer_evidence: Egg: a 2026 meta-analysis of three small trials (326 women) reported higher live birth in poor responders (OR 2.28) [anut-schutz2026], whereas a 2026 RCT in poor responders found more oocytes but no difference in pregnancy [anut-abdelrahman2026]; ESHRE still does not recommend antioxidant add-ons [anut-eshre2023]. Sperm: a 2025 meta-analysis reported clinical pregnancy OR 6.02 from 9 small studies [anut-bakri2025], an implausibly large effect, while broader 2025 and 2022 syntheses found no pregnancy or live-birth benefit from any supplement [anut-michaelsen2025, anut-deligny2022].
audit.bottom_line: CoQ10 is the most promising egg-quality supplement, but the live-birth evidence is three small trials; it is reasonable to try in poor responders, not proven.

audit.claim: Carnitines improve sperm motility and morphology in small trials with no pregnancy effect; the main positive female RCT is retracted.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials [anut-khaw2020]; the PCOS trial was retracted [anut-ismail2014, anut-ejogrb2023] and the Cochrane female review included later-retracted trials [anut-showell2020].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis again found carnitine improves motility but no supplement improves pregnancy or live birth [anut-michaelsen2025]. Carnitine is converted by gut microbes to TMAO, which accelerated atherosclerosis in mice [anut-koeth2013], a reason not to take it without a clear indication.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

audit.claim: NAC helps only people with low glutathione, blunts repair signalling in replete people, accelerated tumours in mice; small uncontrolled sperm data; PCOS trials small and biased.
audit.biases: The 49% vs 1% ovulation contrast in the key PCOS trial [anut-rizk2005] is implausible; PCOS trials from few centres carry integrity risk [anut-bordewijk2020, anut-thakker2015].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 RCT in vascular MCI found NAC added nothing to cardiac rehabilitation [anut-gallagher2026]. Mouse data now show NAC promoting metastasis as well as progression [anut-wiel2019]. The low-glutathione responder finding [anut-paschalis2018] has not been replicated in a larger trial.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged; NAC is not a general 'master antioxidant'.

audit.claim: In small Baylor trials ~7 g glycine + 9 g NAC restored glutathione and improved ageing markers, but a 114-person Nestle RCT at lower doses found no glutathione rise.
audit.biases: Single-group positive trials with many outcomes [anut-kumar2023]; the null trial was industry-run at lower doses and shorter duration [anut-lizzo2022]; both sides have commercial interests.
audit.newer_evidence: No independent replication was found through 2026.
audit.bottom_line: Still unproven: the trials are small and the largest one was null.

audit.claim: 3 g glycine at bedtime reduced next-day fatigue in small studies; ITP mouse lifespan +4-6%; no human ageing trials.
audit.biases: Small, single-group sleep studies [anut-bannai2012].
audit.newer_evidence: No new randomized sleep trial was found in 2024-2026 searches; the ITP result stands [anut-miller2019].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

audit.claim: NR and NMN raise blood NAD+, but most trials show no gain in insulin sensitivity, mitochondria or muscle; NR failed in the ITP; no human egg data.
audit.biases: Industry funding, surrogate outcomes and a baseline imbalance in the main positive NMN trial [anut-yoshino2021, anut-brenner2021].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 meta-analysis of 10 small RCTs found only a modest diastolic blood-pressure drop (-2.15 mmHg) [anut-zhang2026b]; the 2025 muscle meta-analysis remains null [anut-prokopidis2025]; ITP null for NR [anut-harrison2021].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged: raises a biomarker, no proven clinical benefit.

audit.claim: Taurine extended mouse lifespan (2023 Science), but a 2025 NIH study found blood taurine does not fall with age in humans; human trials show small BP, glucose and triglyceride effects.
audit.biases: The 'deficiency drives ageing' human evidence was cross-sectional [anut-singh2023]; longitudinal data contradicted it [anut-fernandez2025].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 Malmo cohort (27,786 people, 25 years) found neither dietary nor plasma taurine predicted dementia, and plasma taurine barely tracked intake [anut-zhang2025], further weakening taurine as a human ageing biomarker. Metabolic RCT meta-analysis unchanged [anut-tzang2024].
audit.bottom_line: Up to date; a 2025 cohort also found no link between taurine and dementia.

audit.claim: Higher dietary spermidine tracked with 24% lower mortality per SD, but the 12-month trial of 0.9 mg/day found no benefit; egg data animal-only.
audit.biases: The cohort cannot separate spermidine from the whole-grain, legume and vegetable pattern it marks (residual confounding by overall diet) [anut-kiechl2018].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2024 RCT gave 40 mg/day of pure spermidine (about 40 times the SmartAge dose) for 28 days and found no substantial change in blood or urine polyamines, indicating tight homeostasis [anut-keohane2024], which weakens the rationale that supplements raise body spermidine; SmartAge remains null [anut-schwarz2022].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged; supplements may not even raise circulating spermidine.

site_change.note: Add the 40 mg/day trial showing no rise in circulating polyamines.

audit.claim: Fisetin extended mouse lifespan in one lab but not in the ITP; no placebo-controlled senolytic trial has reported in humans.

audit.claim: MitoQ 20 mg/day improved artery function in two small trials, did not slow Parkinson disease, and slowed recovery after damaging exercise.

audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 RCT of 12 weeks in older adults found MitoQ lowered muscle H2O2 emission capacity but changed neither respiration nor exercise redox signalling [anut-broome2025].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged: a biomarker effect without demonstrated functional benefit.

audit.claim: In company-funded RCTs 500-1000 mg/day improved some muscle endurance or strength measures and lowered CRP, but most primary endpoints were missed.
audit.biases: All major trials sponsored by the manufacturer; primary endpoints null [anut-liu2022, anut-singh2022].

audit.claim: With resistance training 3-5 g/day adds ~1.4 kg lean mass in older adults; memory effects small and contested; neurodegeneration trials null.
audit.biases: Safety and position statements come partly from industry-linked sports-nutrition authors [anut-kreider2017]; the memory meta-analysis was criticised for double counting [anut-prokopidis2023, anut-eckert2023].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2024 meta-analysis again found small memory gains (SMD 0.31) [anut-xu2024]; muscle and null-neuroprotection findings are unchanged [anut-chilibeck2017, anut-ninds2015].

audit.claim: Enhanced-absorption curcumin modestly lowers CRP and MDA and eases knee-osteoarthritis pain like an NSAID in short trials, but trials are small and low quality, the field has integrity problems, and liver injury is documented.
audit.biases: Curcumin is a PAINS/IMPS compound with poor bioavailability [anut-nelson2017]; meta-analyses pool small, heterogeneous, often single-country trials, and an overview rated 37 of 48 knee-OA outcomes extremely low quality [anut-chen2025]. Larger Western trials are often null [anut-kocher2016].
audit.newer_evidence: Pooled CRP and OA estimates [anut-dehzad2023, anut-wang2021] are unchanged; a 2025 network meta-analysis ranked curcumin top for oocyte outcomes in infertile women, but at very-low certainty [anut-du2025], an example of rankings built on weak trials.
audit.bottom_line: Short trials of enhanced-absorption curcumin show modest CRP and knee-pain benefits, but the trials are small and low quality, the field has integrity problems, and liver injury is documented.
